title: Negative forms and adjectives in the past
summary: ない is an い-adjective meaning "is not", and it builds every negative. い-adjectives make their past with かった.

blocks.text: Everything negative in Japanese is built on one word: **ない**. It is an **い-adjective** meaning "does not exist" or "is not". The picture: **doing** something is a verb, but **not doing** it is a **state**, so it takes an adjective as its engine.
The copula works the same way. だ becomes **ではない** (で is the て-form of だ, plus は for emphasis, plus ない). In speech it is often じゃない.
Attach ない to the **あ-stem** of the verb: change the last kana to its **あ** sound. The one exception is verbs ending in う, which use **わ**. Ichidan verbs just drop る.

Change the final **い** to **く**, then add ない: 赤い → **赤くない**. The same く form also makes the て-form (赤くて). For the **past**, change い to **かった**: 怖い → **怖かった** (it was scary). The negative past of anything is **なかった**.

blocks.jp: さくらが走らなかった。
さくらが走っていなかった。

blocks.text: **ます** has its own negative, **ません** (not ますない). And **いい** (good) uses its old stem **よい** for every change: **よかった** (it was good), **よくない** (not good). Never いくない or いかった.

items: **ない** is an い-adjective: it changes like one (**なかった**, **なくて**).
Verb: **あ-stem + ない** (う-verbs use **わ**); ichidan: drop る.
い-adjective: **い → くない**; past **い → かった**.
Noun / copula: **ではない**; polite verb: **ません**.
**いい → よくない / よかった**.

questions.note: Ichidan verbs drop る and add ない.
う-verbs use わ in front of ない.
い becomes く, then ない.
